analysis.one_liner: Requires labels on genetically engineered food, meat, and poultry products.
analysis.headline: The bill won 31 cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare food misbranded unless it carries a clear label saying it contains or was produced with genetically engineered material, including meat and poultry from animals fed or treated with such material. It would require periodic testing along the supply chain to verify label accuracy, set civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation, and let citizens sue to enforce the rules. Restaurants, deli and takeout foods, and medical foods would be exempt, and foods with trace amounts of one percent or less would be treated as unlabeled-eligible.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who want to know what is in their food, including people with allergies, religious or ethical dietary restrictions, and buyers of organic products, who would get a federally regulated standard for non-engineered claims.

how_it_helps.text: Food containing or produced with a genetically engineered material could not be sold without a conspicuous 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' notice on the package.

The bill defines the duty broadly enough to cover meat and poultry from animals that were fed or injected with genetically engineered material, so labels would reach feed-driven products, not just engineered ingredients themselves.
The government would be required to periodically test foods moving through the chain of distribution to verify that labels are accurate, using the best available testing technology.
Violators face civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, and any person could file a citizen suit to enforce the labeling rules after giving the Secretary 60 days' notice.

Labels claiming a food is not genetically engineered could not be banned merely because no non-engineered version of that food exists, and could not be forced to carry a statement that such labels say nothing about safety.

The bill's findings note that key trading partners including the European Union, Japan, and China had adopted or were implementing mandatory labeling, and argue US labeling would help American producers market to those customers.

analysis.who_pays: Biotech seed developers, food manufacturers, and meat and poultry producers, who would bear labeling, supply-chain segregation, and testing compliance costs, some of which likely pass through to prices at the register.

drawbacks.text: The definition covers animals fed genetically engineered feed, which means virtually all conventional corn- and soy-fed meat, dairy, and eggs would need labels; the compliance cost of segregating supply chains would fall on producers and be partly passed to consumers.
Restaurants and foods prepared in retail establishments, a large share of what Americans eat, would be exempt, so the label would not appear on much of the food people actually consume.

The testing mandate applies only where the Secretary has identified a validated testing method, and a trace amount of one percent or less counts as clean, leaving room for the label's precision to depend heavily on later regulations.
Downstream sellers who accept a good-faith guarantee from a supplier are exempt from penalties, which shifts enforcement risk back up the chain and could make proving violations harder.

Labeling opponents have long argued that a 'genetically engineered' label would stigmatize foods that regulators have treated as safe, which is a cost even supporters must weigh against the value of disclosure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward disclosure of information that most other wealthy countries already require, backed by testing and real penalties. The main costs are compliance: segregating engineered and non-engineered supply chains, especially for animals raised on engineered feed, would be expensive and would nudge food prices upward. The bill is more sweeping than later state-level GMO labeling laws because of the feed provision, and its exemptions for restaurants and deli foods limit how complete the disclosure would be. On balance it is a consumer-information bill with real but bounded costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees and then to a Health subcommittee, but neither committee ever scheduled action, and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on December 2, 2011, joined by 11 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and a week later to Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee.
The bill accumulated 31 cosponsors, 30 Democrats and 1 Republican.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the last action is the December 9, 2011 subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ag-biotech seed developers and packaged-food and meat producers avoided the labeling, testing, and penalty regime; shoppers who wanted the disclosure never got it, and the issue later moved to state ballot fights instead.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 31 cosponsors, framing it as a consumer right-to-know measure.

for.name: 30 House Democrats and 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 30 of the 31 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Republican majority leadership
against.role: Speaker and committee chairs who control the House schedule
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committees and never allowed it a hearing, markup, or floor vote; no action occurred after the December 9, 2011 subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any recorded hearing or markup for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Ag-biotech and packaged-food industries
against.role: Producers of genetically engineered seeds and foods containing them
against.what_they_did: Campaigns against mandatory GMO labeling, in this period most visibly around the 2012 California labeling ballot measure, kept the issue politically difficult in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 original cosponsors and 30 of the 31 total cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.note: Mandatory labeling would apply to the crops their seeds produce and, through the feed provision, to most commodity-fed livestock, undermining the quiet default of unlabeled engineered food. The bill died, so their position remained unchanged.

They would have faced labeling, supply-chain verification, testing, and civil penalties, and had lobbied against labeling mandates; the industry's interest in keeping labels off ran against shoppers' interest in disclosure.

The bill would force labels on animals fed or treated with engineered material, which describes most conventional livestock, creating segregation costs; but producers aiming at export markets that require labeling could benefit from a federal standard.

Certified organic foods are exempt from testing and the bill regulates non-engineered claims, giving the organic sector a federally backed way to verify and market its distinction from engineered food.
The bill explicitly exempts restaurant food and foods prepared in retail establishments, sparing a large segment of the food economy from any labeling duty.
